document.title: Ambassador Dean Cable. "Subject: Letter from Prime Minister Gandhi for President Reagan"
document.authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: Gandhi hands Dean a letter for Reagan outlining India's position on Afghanistan, protesting the Senate Appropriations amendment equating Indian and Pakistani nuclear programs, and stating it is in both countries' interest to avoid fundamentalists gaining the upper hand in Afghanistan.

mentions.quote: THE PRIME MINISTER CALLED ME TO HIS HOUSE AT 7 O'CLOCK LOCAL TIME TO HAND ME A LETTER ADDRESSED TO THE PRESIDENT.
DEAR MR. PRESIDENT: I THANK YOU FOR THE WARM SENTIMENTS EXPRESSED IN YOUR LETTER OF NOVEMBER 2.
THE HON'BLE RONALD REAGAN PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
I AM ASKING AMBASSADOR DEAN TO CONVEY TO YOU SOME OF THESE CONCERNS.

events.description: Rajiv Gandhi hands Ambassador Dean a letter for Reagan on Afghanistan and Pakistan's nuclear program.
Soviet Premier Ryzhkov visited India and discussed Afghanistan with Gandhi.
Talks between Vorontsov and Armacost in Geneva on Afghanistan.
Gandhi handed Ambassador Dean a letter for Reagan about Afghanistan and Pakistan's nuclear program.
Gandhi's letter discusses a coalition government in Afghanistan, Soviet withdrawal, Pakistan's nuclear quest, and opposition to the Senate amendment.
Reagan sent a letter to Gandhi.
Soviet Premier Ryzhkov visited India and discussed Afghanistan with Gandhi.
Vorontsov and Armacost held talks in Geneva on Afghanistan.
Reagan and Gorbachev were soon to sign a treaty and hold a summit.

sources_cited: Declassified State Department cable, New Delhi, 4 December 1987
key_claims: India sought a broad-based coalition government in Afghanistan reflecting realities on the ground.
Gandhi wanted liberal, moderate and democratic forces influential and feared fundamentalist elements gaining the upper hand in Afghanistan.
Ryzhkov told Gandhi the Soviet Union wanted an early troop withdrawal and a balanced representative coalition government.
Gandhi warned that Pakistan's quest for nuclear weapons endangered regional peace and criticized proposed US Senate legislation.
Gandhi had informal exchanges with Afghan leaders in the present government as part of India's outreach.
